`θεμελιόω` is rendered by the support phrase *didst lay the foundation*, whose supplied determiner and auxiliary ride inside the unit under rules 7 and 9. Rule 17's support/light-verb clause heads it on the meaning-bearing complement *foundation*, as *make straight* heads on *straight*. Rule 91's operational test confirms this: the lemma's other corpus units spend *grounded* (EPH.3.17) and *establish* (1PE.5.10), neither of which stands here, so rule 104 sends the query to the root family, where `θεμέλιος` is *foundation* throughout — *foundation* is what carries the lexeme and *lay* is the light verb. A head on *lay* is the competing reading and would be defensible only if *lay* were read as glossing the lexeme.

Rule 21's shape: the article takes the English determiner and the *of* in front of it rides with it, headed on *the* under rule 17. Note that the *of* does not realize this article's case — `τὴν γῆν` is an accusative object and English marks no accusative with *of*; it is licensed by the support frame *lay the foundation of*. The competing reading is therefore to put *of* inside that frame's unit (*didst lay the foundation of*) and leave the article a bare *the*, as rule 91's TIT.3.2 `βλασφημεῖν` → *to speak evil of* does. I took the article reading because rule 67's article-carrier clause hands a determiner-bearing article the whole frame including its trailing *of* even where the case is accusative and does not license it — `τὴν χάριν` → *in regard of this* — and because TIT.3.2 had no determiner-bearing article competing for the word.

review_notes: Every unit's source and target membership, status and head is unchanged from the accepted alignment; the correction is confined to notes. The partition was already complete and correct — all 16 source ids and all 22 target ids appear exactly once.

The `τήν` unit's note previously described *of* as a case preposition. It is not: `τὴν γῆν` is the accusative object of `ἐθεμελίωσας`, and English marks no accusative with *of*. The *of* is licensed by the support frame *lay the foundation of*, which makes its placement a materially contested edge that rule 16 requires the note to name. The competing reading puts *of* inside the verb's unit (*didst lay the foundation of*) and leaves `τήν` a bare *the*, on the model of rule 91's TIT.3.2 `βλασφημεῖν` → *to speak evil of*. The article reading was kept because rule 67's article-carrier clause hands a determiner-bearing article a supplied frame's trailing *of* even where the case does not license it (`τὴν χάριν` → *in regard of this*, also accusative), and because TIT.3.2 had no determiner-bearing article competing for that word.

The head of `ἐθεμελίωσας` is the other contested point and the note now settles it by rule 91's operational test rather than by rule 17 alone: the lemma's corpus units spend *grounded* (EPH.3.17) and *establish* (1PE.5.10), neither of which appears here, so rule 104 sends the query to the root family, where `θεμέλιος` is *foundation*. That is positive evidence for *foundation* over *lay*, which the accepted note lacked.

The two articles of this verse are decided differently, and deliberately: `τήν` before `γῆν` takes the determiner under rule 21, while `τῶν` before `χειρῶν` is `unrepresented` under rule 20 because `σου` is free — rule 76's availability test — to take *thy*. A reference comparison will report the empty `τῶν` as a disagreement, and that report is not a correction.

`κατ᾿ ἀρχάς` is split rather than compounded because rule 94's precondition is a single English word and the ASV wrote three; `οἱ οὐρανοί` and `ἔργα` are crossed relative to the Greek order by the ASV's inversion of a fronted predicate nominal, which rule 15 permits, and no intervening word is absorbed. The vocative's move to second position is the same permission.

Rule 36: the English preposition governing the interrogative phrase is what realizes the Greek preposition, so the first *of* is `πρός` and not part of the verb.
Interrogative pronoun rendered *which*; it carries content of its own, so rule 64 does not touch it.
Rule 21: the partitive *of* plus the determiner form one unit on the article, headed on *the*.
Head noun, left bare by rule 21.
Rule 9: auxiliary and inverted subject ride with the verb, headed on the lexical *said*.

The indefinite temporal adverb takes the whole English frame *at any time*, headed on *time*, the word rendering the adverb's temporal sense. *any* is the competing head, rendering the indefiniteness, and would be defensible on the analogy of rule 69's `οὐδένα` → *any man* headed on *any*; I take *time* because nothing here is a generic completion — `ποτέ` is temporal and *time* is what carries that.
Imperative with its supplied subject pronoun as a rule 7 helper, headed on the verb.
The ASV spreads the phrase over separate words, so rule 94 splits it and the preposition takes its own *on*.
Genitive pronoun carrying the possessive *my*.
Substantival adjective expanded with the generic noun *hand*; rule 17's generic-noun clause holds the head on the adjective.

Rule 50 refuses to leave `ἄν` `unrepresented`, and the ASV writes a single *Till* for `ἕως ἄν`, with no modal and no *-soever* for the particle to answer to separately. So the pair is one aligned unit under rule 39's test, some part of the English (*Till*) answering to `ἕως` — the treatment rule 50 gives a relative compressed with `ἄν` into one word. Giving *Till* to `ἕως` alone and marking `ἄν` `unrepresented` is the competing reading, and rule 50 names it as the recurring failure.
Rule 9: supplied subject pronoun rides with the verb, headed on the lexical *make*.
Rule 20: the genitive `σου` is present and free and carries *thine*, so this article realizes nothing.
Substantival adjective rendered *enemies*.
Rule 20: genitive pronoun takes the possessive.
Anarthrous noun; rule 51's anarthrous clause makes the supplied *the* a rule 7 helper on it.
Rule 20: `σου` carries *thy*, so the article governing `ποδῶν` realizes nothing and the case preposition *of* stays with the noun.
Discontinuous under rule 15, the possessive standing between; rule 20 leaves *of* with the noun.
Rule 20: genitive pronoun takes the possessive.

review_notes: The two contested units are `ἕως ἄν` → *Till*, joined rather than leaving `ἄν` empty as rule 50 requires, and the head of *at any time*; both notes name the competing reading.
Three of the four articles are emptied by a free genitive `σου` under rule 20; only `τῶν` before `ἀγγέλων` takes an English determiner, and under rule 21 it takes the partitive *of* with it.
`ἐκ δεξιῶν μου` is spread over separate English words, so rule 94 forbids a compound unit and each token stands on its own.

alignments.note: Expressed copula εἰσίν → 'Are'. The supplied subject pronoun goes to the expressed Greek subject πάντες, not here: rule 9 licenses a subject on a finite verb, but this clause expresses its subject, and the chapter puts the subject word on the expressed token throughout (1:5 αὐτός → 'he' beside ἔσται → 'shall be', 1:11 σύ → 'thou' beside διαμένεις, 1:12 σύ → 'thou' beside εἶ → 'art'). The inversion that writes 'Are they' together is English word order, which rules 53 and 63 refuse as a licence.
Rule 64: οὐχί carries content of its own and is aligned in the ordinary way, as 'not'; it is not a bare question marker for rule 44 to empty.

Substantival quantifier subject → 'they … all', the supplied pronoun a rule 7 helper on it exactly as at 1:11's 'they all', discontinuous around 'not' under rule 15 and headed on 'all'. Corrected from the accepted reading, which gave 'they' to εἰσίν. The competing reading is the corpus's εἰμί → 'are they', but those six units stand in clauses expressing no subject, whereas πάντες is the expressed masculine nominative subject here. Rule 87 does not join the quantifier to οὐχί: the ASV writes two English words, which rule 87's closing clause leaves to the ordinary split.
Attributive adjective rendered 'ministering', split from its noun under rule 26.
Predicate noun, anarthrous and given no determiner.
Participle rendered 'sent forth', the particle belonging to the English verb rather than to the preposition, which stands elsewhere in the clause.

Purpose εἰς realized by the word introducing its English clause, the infinitival 'to', under rules 36 and 40. Rule 61's bare-infinitive clause is not the case here, since a preposition is expressed for the 'to' to answer to; leaving εἰς unrepresented and giving 'to do service' whole to the noun is the competing reading, and rule 36 refuses it because English does realize the preposition.

The supplied 'do' is an empty support verb selected by the noun — you 'do' service as you 'bear' witness and 'give' thanks — so rule 7 gives it to the word that licenses it and rule 91's support-verb clause makes it a helper on the meaning-bearing complement, headed on 'service' under rule 17. Rule 62 is not the case: it is scoped to a verbless Greek clause whose prepositional phrase is the predicate, and this clause expresses εἰσίν while εἰς διακονίαν modifies ἀποστελλόμενα.

Rule 67's complex frame 'for the sake of', carried whole by the expressed preposition. Rule 67 leaves the head open for a proper preposition, and the prepositional word is taken on rule 46's stated test — the identical English heads on 'sake' or 'cause' only for the postposition χάριν, and on the prepositional word wherever a Greek preposition is expressed — which is also how rule 78 settles the discontinuous 'for … sake' wrap. A head on 'sake' is the competing reading and stands in the corpus for a contiguous frame on a proper preposition elsewhere.

Rule 32: a substantival article before a participle supplies the pronoun and nothing else, so it takes 'them' alone and the relativizer stays with the participle. Rule 90 is not in question, the ASV writing two English words for the pair.

μέλλω is realized by the futurity auxiliary 'shall', and the supplied relativizer 'that' is its rule 7 helper under rule 32. Headed on 'shall' because that is the word realizing this lexeme, not on the relativizer; rule 17's preference for a lexical verb over an auxiliary does not reach inside a unit whose only lexical realization is the auxiliary.
Complementary infinitive; the English infinitival marker is absorbed into the 'shall' periphrasis, so the verb stands on its own word.
Object noun.

review_notes: One edge moved: t002 'they' from εἰσίν to πάντες. εἰσίν keeps 'Are' and its head; πάντες keeps its head on 'all'. All 13 source ids and all 20 target ids remain partitioned exactly once.

The competing reading is the corpus's εἰμί → 'are they' (2CO.11.22 twice and four others, headed on 'are'). It does not carry here: those clauses express no subject, so the pronoun has nothing but the verb to belong to, whereas πάντες is the expressed masculine nominative subject of this clause and πνεύματα the neuter predicate.
The discontinuity is between 'they' and 'all' only; 'not' stays with οὐχί and no intervening word is absorbed.
Rule 87 is still not in question: the ASV writes the negation and the quantification as two separate English words, which rule 87's closing clause leaves to the ordinary split.

The rest of the verse is left exactly as the verse pass returned it, including 'do' on διακονίαν rather than on εἰς, and the head of διά → 'for the sake of' on 'for' with 'sake' named as the competing reading.
